section_summary: This section consists chiefly of public appeals asking the Roosevelt administration to halt American exports of arms, scrap iron, petroleum, aircraft, and other war-related supplies to Japan during the Sino-Japanese War. The Department of State repeatedly explains that the Neutrality Act would embargo arms to both China and Japan only after a presidential finding of a state of war, and that existing law did not authorize restrictions on raw materials such as scrap iron. Enclosures include petitions, missionary eyewitness accounts of Japanese bombing in China, congressional referrals, replies from the State and War Departments, and cross-reference sheets concerning German credit and scrap-metal shipments to Japan.

keywords: Office of Arms and Munitions Control

subfiles.title: Conclusion of Department of State response to British aide-mémoire
subfiles.about: Concludes a statement on American policy principles and anticipated British measures concerning relations among states.
subfiles.summary: Conclusion of State's reply to the British aide-memoire: it keeps studying ways to secure respect for its principles and expects Britain to keep it informed of steps under the October 20 aide-memoire.

subfiles.title: Merrill F. Clarke to Cordell Hull on exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Questions the administration's argument against refusing exports used in Japan's conquest of China.
subfiles.summary: Merrill Clarke thanks Hull for statistics showing lower September arms licenses to Japan, rejects that refusing war materials would lead to war, and finds soliciting China relief from factory owners supplying Japan uncomfortable.

subfiles.title: Richard B. Carter to Charles W. Yost on the Neutrality Act
subfiles.about: Asks why the President has not formally found that a state of war exists in China.
subfiles.summary: Richard Carter argues the Neutrality Act seems to require a proclamation when war exists, asks whether the administration denies war in China or reads the law as allowing an interest-based decision, and asks the statistics' end date.

subfiles.title: Charles E. Maddry to Cordell Hull forwarding a missionary's letter
subfiles.about: Forwards J. Hundley Wiley's letter and urges an end to American aid for Japan's war in China.
subfiles.summary: Charles Maddry forwards Southern Baptist missionary Wiley's letter and, for the Foreign Mission Board, urges preventing munitions makers from selling war materials to Japan or China.

subfiles.title: J. Hundley Wiley to Charles E. Maddry
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese pressure on the University of Shanghai and condemns American material support for Japan.
subfiles.summary: J. Hundley Wiley encloses an article on Japanese efforts to ruin the University of Shanghai, says settlement promises keep Baptists quiet, and calls aiding Japanese militarists immoral and strategically foolish.

subfiles.title: Department of State reply to Charles E. Maddry
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Wiley's letter and explains why the Neutrality Act has not been invoked against both China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply thanks Maddry for conveying the Foreign Mission Board's views. It explains that a presidential proclamation under the Neutrality Act would immediately prohibit arms exports to both belligerents and says the President exercised statutory discretion after considering the act's purpose of keeping the United States out of war.

subfiles.title: Frederick B. Stewart to President Roosevelt forwarding a church appeal
subfiles.about: Forwards a unanimously authorized appeal from a Methodist quarterly conference.
subfiles.summary: Frederick Stewart forwards to Roosevelt a Washington Park Methodist church appeal directed by its unanimous quarterly conference; the White House referred it for acknowledgment.

subfiles.title: Washington Park Methodist Episcopal Church appeal to the President
subfiles.from: Washington Park Methodist Episcopal Church Quarterly Conference
subfiles.about: Urges the President to end American traffic sustaining the war against China.
subfiles.summary: Church asks Roosevelt to use every power against commerce that makes the U.S. a partner in the Far Eastern conflict, citing destruction in China and friendly relations.

subfiles.title: Joseph C. Green to Frederick B. Stewart
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the statutory limits of the Neutrality Act and supplies arms-export totals for China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green tells Stewart a proclamation would embargo arms to China and Japan, no authority exists otherwise, other commodities aren't covered; licenses since July 1, 1937 total about $14.27 million for China and $10.79 million for Japan.

subfiles.title: Dorothy Canfield Fisher to Charles W. Yost
subfiles.about: Thanks Yost for his explanation of the munitions embargo question.
subfiles.summary: Dorothy Canfield Fisher will present Yost's detailed letter to Vermont peace groups, who asked her to raise the question with the President.

subfiles.title: Dorothy Canfield Fisher and others to President Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Dorothy Canfield Fisher and other Vermont peace activists
subfiles.about: Asks why arms are embargoed to Republican Spain while munitions and scrap iron may be exported to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Fisher and others of a Women's International League branch can't reconcile the Spanish embargo with unrestricted exports to Japan, reject rumors of munitions-industry pressure, and ask the President for an authoritative explanation.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost to Dorothy Canfield Fisher
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Contrasts the legal bases of the Spanish arms embargo and the administration's policy in the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Yost tells Fisher Congress imposed the Spanish embargo in January 1937, whereas the general Neutrality Act would embargo both China and Japan; the President judged invocation not in the national interest; arms-license totals given.

subfiles.title: Frederick B. Moss to President Roosevelt forwarding South Church resolution
subfiles.about: Forwards a parish petition opposing American assistance to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Frederick Moss sends Roosevelt South Church's appeal signed after the October 16 service, not by name-to-name solicitation but reflecting the congregation.

subfiles.title: South Church petition against war-related exports to Japan
subfiles.to: President and Congress of the United States
subfiles.about: Petitions for every practicable measure to end American traffic supporting Japan's invasion of China.
subfiles.summary: The resolution condemns Japanese aggression, bombing of undefended cities, and destruction of civilian and foreign property. It declares that American aircraft, shells, scrap iron, oil, trucks, and raw materials are sustaining the war and asks the President and Congress to terminate that traffic.

subfiles.title: Joseph C. Green to Frederick B. Moss
subfiles.about: Responds to the South Church resolution with the administration's standard legal explanation.
subfiles.summary: Green tells Moss the Neutrality Act could embargo arms to both countries only after a proclamation and gives no power over other goods; license totals given, and the government has discouraged aircraft makers from encouraging civilian bombing.

subfiles.title: I. A. Smothers to Cordell Hull forwarding missionary correspondence
subfiles.about: Forwards missionary correspondence describing civilian suffering in China and asks that it receive official attention.
subfiles.summary: I. A. Smothers forwards former pupil Florence Schafer's missionary material from India, appealing to Hull's humanitarian concern; his congregation also asked him to bring it to Roosevelt.

subfiles.title: Gladys Stephenson letter from the Hospital of Universal Love
subfiles.about: Gives an eyewitness account of bombing casualties, hospital work, and missionary endurance in Hankou and Wuchang.
subfiles.summary: Gladys Stephenson, at the Hospital of Universal Love, describes mass air-raid casualties, emergency surgery, American and British markings on bomb fragments, preparations for Hankou's invasion, and nurses' determination to stay; it ends with lines from "The Dawn."

subfiles.title: Joseph C. Green to I. A. Smothers
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the missionary letters and restates the legal and policy position on exports and civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: Green notes that the Department had already received similar correspondence from Florence Schafer and had asked the American consular officer at Bombay to provide her with information. He explains the Neutrality Act's limits, gives arms-license totals, and describes the government's condemnation of civilian bombing and representations to aircraft exporters.

subfiles.title: B. A. Drum to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Asks why the President does not prohibit arms and ammunition sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: B. A. Drum, a 74-year-old Roosevelt voter, cites his role with Chamberlain in the Czechoslovak crisis and asks him to stop the slaughter of Chinese civilians.

subfiles.title: Joseph C. Green to B. A. Drum
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains why the President has not invoked the Neutrality Act against China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green says a proclamation would stop arms exports to both countries and that no statutory prohibition exists without one. He cites presidential discretion, the objective of keeping the United States out of war, and licensed-export totals for China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Harry H. Woodring to the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Transmits Mrs. Fred Schneider's letter, petition, and a copy of the War Department's reply.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of War Woodring forwards Mrs. Schneider's materials to State for appropriate consideration, with his reply to her.

subfiles.title: Mrs. Fred Schneider to Harry H. Woodring
subfiles.about: Forwards a petition against exports to Japan and asks where trade statistics can be obtained.
subfiles.summary: Schneider sends an enclosure that she believes should receive Woodring's attention and offers personal praise and good wishes. She asks for a response and for information on obtaining statistics concerning the proportion of goods shipped abroad.

subfiles.title: Seattle petition against exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Protests the sale and shipment to Japan of raw materials and implements usable in warfare.
subfiles.summary: The petitioners ask the President to use the powers of his office to prevent shipments to Japan of arms, ammunition, raw materials, and other war-related goods. The petition is followed by names and Seattle addresses, with an additional largely illegible page.

subfiles.title: Harry H. Woodring to Mrs. Fred Schneider
subfiles.about: Refers Schneider's petition to the State Department and directs her to the Commerce Department for export statistics.
subfiles.summary: Woodring tells Mrs. Schneider the petition is State's jurisdiction, gives the Seattle Commerce representative's contact, and notes Army arsenals differ from commercial munitions factories.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost to Mrs. Fred Schneider
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Replies to the petition referred by the Secretary of War and explains the limits of export-control authority.
subfiles.summary: Yost states that invoking the Neutrality Act would embargo arms to both China and Japan, while the act does not authorize controls over other commodities. He cites presidential discretion and provides licensed-export totals for the two countries.

subfiles.title: Millard E. Tydings to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Forwards Sam Weinblatt's letter and requests information concerning its second paragraph.
subfiles.summary: Senator Tydings asks State to note Weinblatt's views and return the letter with available information.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull to Millard E. Tydings
subfiles.about: Reports that the Department had already received a similar letter from Weinblatt and supplies its reply and related materials.
subfiles.summary: Hull tells Tydings Weinblatt wrote directly and encloses the reply, the July 1 letter to manufacturers, press releases and the arms-traffic pamphlet.

subfiles.title: E. N. Hamilton to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Urges implementation of Roosevelt's quarantine policy through a boycott of munitions, oil, and war materials destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: E. N. Hamilton says sales of scrap, aircraft, oil, metals and munitions help Japan close China's Open Door, calls it complicity in China's crucifixion, and asks whether a boycott could avert moral bankruptcy.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost to E. N. Hamilton
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Hamilton's renewed appeal concerning exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost notes Hamilton's letter came by White House referral and directs him to the Department's November 4 reply on the same subject.

subfiles.title: T. S. McFerrin to Cordell Hull forwarding a missionary-society resolution
subfiles.about: Forwards names gathered in support of a resolution against assisting Japan's war in China.
subfiles.summary: T. S. McFerrin, for the Memphis Conference Methodist Woman's Missionary Society, links the appeal to its support for China missionaries and encloses signed resolution sheets.

subfiles.title: Memphis missionary-society resolution and signatures
subfiles.from: Members of the Missionary Society of the First Methodist Church, Memphis
subfiles.to: President and Congress of the United States
subfiles.about: Calls for action preventing American materials and financial resources from aiding Japan's aggression in China.
subfiles.summary: The repeated resolution states that Japan's armed forces have invaded China and that supplies bought in America are inflicting suffering and loss of life and property. Five pages carry the resolution and numerous handwritten signatures and addresses.

subfiles.title: Joseph C. Green to T. S. McFerrin
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the signed Methodist resolution and explains American neutrality and export law.
subfiles.summary: Green states that a presidential proclamation would embargo arms to both belligerents but that existing law does not permit restrictions on other commodities. He supplies arms-license totals and describes the Department's condemnation of civilian bombing and its representations to aircraft manufacturers.

subfiles.title: Elyria church-school pupils to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: Bill Henderson and other church-school pupils
subfiles.about: Eleven-year-old pupils ask Hull to stop fighting in China and halt scrap-iron sales used to make Japanese bombs.
subfiles.summary: Elyria church-school pupils, supporting missionaries in China and Japan, heard Japan bombs mission schools and ask Hull to end the fighting and scrap exports.

subfiles.title: Joseph C. Green to Bill Henderson
subfiles.about: Explains to the pupils that the Neutrality Act excludes scrap iron from presidential export controls.
subfiles.summary: Green praises the class's interest in international affairs but says no existing statute authorizes the President or Secretary of State to prohibit scrap-iron exports. He also outlines the government's condemnation of civilian bombing and its representations to aircraft and aeronautical-equipment exporters.

subfiles.title: Pierce County Workers Alliance to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: Margaret Mock for Local 11, Workers Alliance of Pierce County
subfiles.about: Appeals for an end to shipments of scrap iron and other war supplies from Tacoma to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Pierce County Workers Alliance says scrap iron is being loaded at Tacoma for Japan and asks Hull to curb profiteering and end U.S. participation in an undeclared war on China.

subfiles.title: Joseph C. Green to Margaret Mock
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Responds that the Neutrality Act cannot prohibit scrap-iron exports and would embargo arms to both China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green explains why the President has not issued a state-of-war proclamation and emphasizes that the law covers only enumerated arms, ammunition, and implements of war. Scrap iron is outside those categories, and no current statute authorizes its prohibition; the letter also gives export-license totals.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Peiping despatch on German loan to Japan
subfiles.about: Refers researchers to a despatch concerning a German loan for Japanese munitions and war materials.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Peiping despatch 1734 on a Manchukuo Embassy secretary's statements about a 170-million-yen German loan for munitions, file 716.93 Manchuria/3.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Hong Kong despatch on scrap-metal shipments
subfiles.about: Refers researchers to a despatch reporting scrap-metal shipments from Hong Kong to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Hong Kong report on scrap-metal shipments to Japan, file 8466.24/4.

subfiles.title: Allen T. Treadway to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Forwards Susie A. Johnson's appeal for enforcement of American neutrality laws in the China conflict.
subfiles.summary: Allen Treadway encloses a constituent's November 14 letter and asks Hull's response on neutrality at his convenience.

subfiles.title: Susie A. Johnson to Allen T. Treadway
subfiles.about: Argues that American petroleum, aircraft, and vehicles enable Japan to continue the war in China.
subfiles.summary: Susie Johnson learned Japan depends heavily on American gasoline, aircraft and trucks despite declared neutrality, warns a Japan enriched by China could turn on the U.S., and urges enforcing neutrality.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull to Allen T. Treadway
subfiles.about: Provides suggested language and enclosures for answering Susie A. Johnson's neutrality complaint.
subfiles.summary: Hull explains that a presidential proclamation would embargo arms to both China and Japan and that the Neutrality Act does not cover other commodities. He gives licensed-export totals, reiterates the government's condemnation of civilian bombing, and returns Johnson's letter with the relevant pamphlet and resolution.

subfiles.title: Ernest H. Wilkins to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Urges broader governmental action against exports building Japanese military power.
subfiles.summary: Ernest Wilkins warns Japan mastering China's resources could threaten the Americas, describes shareholders' moral dilemma, and proposes extending the aircraft request to all munitions and raw materials while supporting an official embargo.

subfiles.title: R. Walton Moore to Ernest H. Wilkins
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains why the Department's advisory action was limited to aircraft used in bombing civilians.
subfiles.summary: Moore says manufacturers and exporters substantially complied with the July 1 request concerning military aircraft and equipment. He explains that such advisory intervention was justified by the exceptional and universally condemned practice of aerial bombing of civilians, and notes Wilkins's support for legislation permitting a broader embargo.

subfiles.title: Perry L. Morgan to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Conveys community opposition to Japan's repudiation of international obligations and asks what can be done.
subfiles.summary: Perry Morgan, partly illegibly, cites Japan's conduct toward China, repudiation of the Kellogg-Briand Pact and bombing, and asks what action is possible for his community.

subfiles.title: Joseph C. Green to Perry L. Morgan
subfiles.about: Gives the standard State Department explanation of neutrality law, export licensing, and civilian-bombing policy.
subfiles.summary: Green tells Morgan invoking the Neutrality Act would embargo both China and Japan and the President declined, given its peace-preserving purpose; other commodities aren't covered; license totals and aircraft-exporter representations noted.
